# Recall



* We’re focusing on the interaction of language and \(pop\) culture
  * Language and the media = mediators between worlds\!
  * Language and movies – storytelling\, dialect coaches
* To talk about those\, we needed to talk about
  * Sociolinguistics and linguistic anthropology
  * Cognition and learning theory
* What’s most important about this unit is that nothing we do with language is detached from the rest of what’s going on around us – including our bodies\, our societies\, and our pop worlds\!

# Create your own?



* One of the key things we have said about language is that it is  _acquired_ \, which suggests something that happens to a human naturally
* Languages that are used in the “real world” are called  __natural languages __ \(sometimes  __natlang__  for short\)
* But\, in “fictional world\(s\)”\, we may run across  __constructed languages __ \(or  __conlangs __ for short\)
  * Conlangs are any language that has been consciously created
  * These might be like Dothraki from  _Game of Thrones _ or various languages in the  _Star Wars _ and  _Marvel _ franchises\, for example
  * We can also call these kind of languages  __fictional languages__
  * Not all conlangs are just in fictional worlds though – languages like Esperanto exist

# Why would we make our own?



* Aside from the Hollywood angle\, one might make another language to:
  * Help make communication easier \(like making what’s called an  __international auxiliary language__ \, which can be used by people who speak other languages when they need to communicate; kind of like a  __lingua franca__ \) = Esperanto
  * Experiment with what is possible within the areas of linguistics\, cognitive science\, and machine learning
  * Make a game\! As a hobby\!
* As we’ll see\, they require a lot of work\, so very few gain a lot of traction beyond their original creation reason
  * Esperanto has gained a bit of ground over time\, but no other  __planned__  languages have really caught on
  * With the advent of the internet\, fans have been more particular about having “good” languages in their films and shows \(and will drag producers online if they don’t\)

  * Rules about sentence structure
  * Pragmatics
  * Writing system \(maybe\)
  * Etc\.\, etc\.\, etc\.


# What do you need?


---




* Here is just a small list of things you would need to decide about your language:
  * Which consonants/vowels?
  * How do you make syllables?
  * What are the rules about putting sounds together?
  * Is your language stress\-based or tonal?
  * How would someone know you were asking a question?
  * What parts of speech?
  * What are the words?
  * How do you mark nouns for number/gender/role?
  * Do adjectives agree?
  * Does it have articles like “the” and “a”?
  * How do you conjugate verbs?
  * Do you mark tense/aspect/mood?
  * What is your language’s word order?

# To be a language…



* You need a self\-contained sound system that is distinct from other languages
  * This is why “Pig Latin” isn’t really a different language
* You need a self\-contained word/sentence system that is distinct from other languages
  * Also why “Pig Latin” isn’t a different language
* It must be systematic…
  * Ubese \( _Star Wars_ \)
  * __Yaté__  __ __  __yaté__  __ __  __yotó__  __\. 					__
  * __I have come for the bounty on this Wookie\. 		__
  * __Yotó__  __ __  __yotó__  __\. __
  * __50\,000\, no less\.__

---


# And…



* Your language will inevitably be embedded in some kind of culture
  * When a character in a movie uses another language\, it is because that person is being represented as belonging to that culture
  * Like with our discussion of movies\, it is important to the character development
  * And it shouldn’t be random\! There will be aspects of your culture that matter to your language
    * Ex\. If your culture is very focused on politeness\, your language will need to have built\-in ways to show deference\, kind of like Japanese does
    * Ex\. If you want to represent a hierarchical society\, you will have standard/proper dialects spoken by those in higher positions and non\-standard versions spoken by people in lower positions

# Writing system

![](images/23-Can%20you%20make%20your%20own%20language_4.png)



* We already talked about the fact that
  * Not all languages are written
  * Writing is learned\, not acquired
  * There are many ways to represent language in writing
  * Writing must represent language \(not pictograms\)
* What does this mean for a conlang?
  * You can use a pre\-existing writing system\!
  * You can make it up altogether\!
  * Remember – the squiggles we make to represent English are just as arbitrary as any other way to represent language\!
  * Must be systematic\!

---


# Media

[https://www\.youtube\.com/watch?v=4xPuxJkMA5o&t=1s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4xPuxJkMA5o&t=1s) \(Byrds\)


---




* Remember – last class\, we were talking about whether actors are good at doing dialects
  * We said that this matters for the sake of a believable story\, even in cases where what is going on is not like our own real worlds
  * E\.g\.\, we need someone who “sounds” like they could come from Africa in a story told about a fictional world where people have super high\-tech weapons that we can’t even begin to dream about making in the real world
* So\, in certain fictional worlds\, it will make the most sense for a culture to have its own language
  * And\, again\, the fan base for many of these fictional universes is huge\, vocal\, and online
  * The success/failure of a franchise may lie in the conlang\!
  * Ok\, so Star Wars had bad ones\, and they did fine\! But those movies \(originally\) pre\-date the internet
  * Things like Game of Thrones were more successful because fans got on board with the languages\!
